q: Why is baking a cake NOT considered a pure information process?
options: It has too few steps to count as a process
It cannot be described as a sequence of steps
It involves physical things such as sugar and flour rather than only abstract information
It does not have a goal
explanation: Baking involves physical materials, so it is a process but not a pure information process. Computer science studies processes on abstract information.

q: Which of these is the best example of a pure information process as computer science uses the term?
options: Sorting a list of student names into alphabetical order
Mailing a letter to a friend
Planting a tree in a garden
Baking a cake for a party
explanation: Sorting names works only on abstract information (text and data). The other three involve physical objects.

q: A key press is physically an electrical signal, yet computer science deliberately ignores such physical details. What reason do the notes give?
options: Physical details are never involved in real computers
Computers are not really physical machines
Physical details can only be studied by engineers
Ignoring them makes computation simpler to understand and reason about
explanation: Computers are physical, but focusing on the information makes computation simpler to understand and reason about.

q: A cook follows a written recipe to make soup. In computer science terms, which statement is correct?
options: The act of cooking is the procedure and the written recipe is the process
The written recipe is the procedure and the act of cooking is the process
Both the recipe and the cooking are procedures
Both the recipe and the cooking are processes
explanation: A procedure is the description of the steps (the recipe). A process is the act of carrying them out (the cooking).

q: Which instruction would prevent a procedure from being a mechanical procedure?
options: Add exactly 2 teaspoons of salt
Repeat the next step 10 times
Add salt until it tastes about right
Stir for 30 seconds
explanation: A mechanical procedure can be followed exactly with no thought or judgment. 'Until it tastes about right' requires judgment.

q: A procedure can be followed exactly with no judgment, but for some inputs it could run forever. How should it be classified?
options: As an algorithm, because it is mechanical
As a mechanical procedure that is not an algorithm, because it is not guaranteed to finish
As a process, because it never ends
As not a procedure at all, because it is not a description of steps
explanation: An algorithm must be both mechanical and guaranteed to eventually finish. Without the guarantee it is only a mechanical procedure.

q: Which statement is NOT true?
options: Every algorithm is a mechanical procedure
An algorithm is guaranteed to eventually finish
A procedure is a description of a process
Every mechanical procedure is an algorithm
explanation: A mechanical procedure that might run forever is not an algorithm, so algorithms are only a subset of mechanical procedures.

q: Which is an unstated assumption in the coffee-making procedure?
options: The coffee beans must be ground by hand
The water must be boiled before it is poured
The filter must be made of metal
The coffeemaker is plugged in and sitting on a flat surface
explanation: The steps never say the coffeemaker must be plugged in and level, but they only work if it is. This shows how natural-language steps rely on unspoken assumptions.

q: Which order of the final steps follows the coffee procedure?
options: Close the lid, put the decanter on the warming plate, press ON
Press ON, close the lid, put the decanter on the warming plate
Put the decanter on the warming plate, press ON, close the lid
Close the lid, press ON, put the decanter on the warming plate
explanation: The procedure closes the lid, then puts the decanter on the warming plate, and presses ON last.

q: Which instruction is the best example of ambiguity in natural language?
options: Press the ON button
Put the cup on the table by the window with the flowers
Open the lid
Place the filter in the basket
explanation: It can be read more than one way (the table with the flowers, or the window with the flowers). Natural language is ambiguous in this way.

q: A computer carries out a process of one trillion steps. Which problem arises if every step is written out as a list?
options: The steps become ambiguous
The computer loses its common sense
The description becomes impossibly long
The process stops being mechanical
explanation: Description length grows with the number of steps. We need a way to describe a huge number of steps briefly.

q: What point do the notes make by mentioning long legal documents?
options: Laws are always unambiguous if they are long enough
Legal documents are examples of algorithms
Only short documents can be written in natural language
Adding more detail helps but natural language stays ambiguous
explanation: Even long, detailed laws are argued over for years, so extra detail does not remove the ambiguity of natural language.

q: Why can a machine not follow the step 'fill the decanter with water' as written?
options: A machine has no common sense, so details such as where the water comes from and how to turn on the faucet must be explained
The step is too long for a machine to read
Machines cannot handle liquids in any procedure
The step is mechanical, and machines only follow non-mechanical steps
explanation: A machine has no common sense, so a procedure for it must be fully detailed.

q: Which set of qualities explains why programmers use programming languages instead of English?
options: They are flexible, informal, and rely on context
They are clear, brief, and fully detailed so a machine can follow them exactly
They are long, detailed, and open to interpretation
They are short, ambiguous, and easy to read aloud
explanation: Programming languages avoid ambiguity, describe many steps briefly, and include all the detail a machine needs.

q: Which statement about programming languages is NOT true?
options: They let us write procedures that are followed exactly as written
They can describe a huge number of steps briefly
They allow the machine to use common sense to fill in missing details
They avoid the ambiguity found in natural languages
explanation: Machines have no common sense, so everything must be spelled out. That is why programming languages are precise and fully detailed.

q: A business video says a procedure is the lowest level of work, such as clicking buttons, and a process is a group of about 5 to 15 tasks. On a computer science exam asking for the definitions, what is the best approach?
options: Use the business meanings, because they are more detailed
Use the CS meanings: a procedure is a description of steps and a process is the act of carrying it out
Say that a procedure is an action and a process is a group of tasks
Treat procedure and process as having the same meaning
explanation: Business process management uses these words differently from computer science. For a CS exam, use the CS definitions.

q: Consider this procedure: set n to 5, then repeat 'subtract 2 from n' until n equals 0. What does this show?
options: n takes the values 3, 1, -1 and so on, never equals 0, and the procedure never finishes, so it is not an algorithm
n becomes 3, then 1, then 0, so the procedure finishes
n reaches 0 after 3 subtractions, so it is an algorithm
n reaches 0 after 2 subtractions, so it is an algorithm
explanation: 5 minus 2 repeatedly gives 3, 1, -1, and so on, which skips 0. Since it is not guaranteed to finish, it is not an algorithm.

q: In business process management, which item would be a procedure, the lowest level?
options: Onboarding a new employee from start to finish
A group of 10 related tasks
Entering the employee's name into the HR form
Approving a company budget
explanation: In business process management, a procedure is the lowest level, such as entering data. A process is the top level, a group of about 5 to 15 tasks.

q: Your course defines computer science one way, but another textbook defines the field more broadly. Which approach is best for this course's exams?
options: Use whichever definition is longer
Use the broader textbook definition
Combine the two definitions into one
Use the definition your course uses
explanation: The notes say different books define the field differently, so you should use the definition your own course uses.

q: Which description best fits a process as defined in the notes?
options: A sequence of steps in which each step changes the state of the world a little, and together they reach a goal
A single action that changes nothing
A list of rules that is never carried out
A physical machine that performs calculations
explanation: A process is a sequence of steps that each change the state of the world a little and together reach a goal.

q: A procedure always stops after at most 100 steps, but one step says 'decide whether the result looks good enough'. Why is it NOT an algorithm?
options: Because it stops too quickly
Because it has too many steps
Because it is written as a list
Because that step needs judgment, so the procedure is not mechanical
explanation: An algorithm must be mechanical and guaranteed to finish. Guaranteed stopping is not enough if a step needs judgment.

q: Which pairing correctly matches the two problems with step lists to what a programming language needs?
options: Ambiguity calls for brevity, and long descriptions call for clarity
Ambiguity calls for common sense, and long descriptions call for more detail
Ambiguity calls for informality, and long descriptions call for more steps
Ambiguity calls for clarity, and long descriptions call for brevity
explanation: Natural language is ambiguous, so a programming language must be clear. Listing every step is too long, so it must be brief.

q: In business process management, as the notes describe it, which ordering runs from the lowest level to the highest?
options: Procedure, task, process
Process, task, procedure
Task, procedure, process
Procedure, process, task
explanation: In that field a procedure is the lowest level, a task is the middle level, and a process is the top level.

q: A person performs random unrelated actions with no ordering and no goal. Why is this NOT a process as the notes define it?
options: It is not a sequence of steps that together reach a goal
It involves too few physical objects
It is not carried out by a machine
It is not written in a programming language
explanation: A process is a sequence of steps that together reach a goal. Random actions with no order or goal do not fit.

q: A student says: My procedure is an algorithm because it finished on every input I tried. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Algorithms must never use inputs
An algorithm must be non-mechanical
Testing some inputs does not guarantee that it will always eventually finish
The procedure must be a process first
explanation: An algorithm must be guaranteed to eventually finish. Finishing on the inputs tried is not a guarantee for all inputs.

q: A recipe card is sitting in a drawer and nobody is cooking. Which statement is correct?
options: The card is a procedure, but no process is happening
The card is a process, and no procedure exists
The card is both a procedure and a process
The card is an algorithm because it exists
explanation: The card is a description of steps (a procedure). A process only happens when someone carries the steps out.

q: Suppose each step is written on its own line and a page holds 50 lines. About how many pages are needed to list a process of 1 trillion steps?
options: 2 billion
20 billion
200 million
200 billion
explanation: 1,000,000,000,000 divided by 50 is 20,000,000,000 pages, or 20 billion. This shows why listing every step is impractical.

q: Which ordering goes from the broadest category to the narrowest?
options: Algorithm, mechanical procedure, procedure
Mechanical procedure, procedure, algorithm
Procedure, mechanical procedure, algorithm
Procedure, algorithm, mechanical procedure
explanation: Every algorithm is a mechanical procedure, and every mechanical procedure is a procedure. So the categories narrow in that order.

q: Which statement is NOT true?
options: Baking a cake is a process
Planting a tree is a pure information process
Planting a tree is a process
Mailing a letter is a process
explanation: Planting a tree is a process, but it involves physical things like dirt, so it is not a pure information process.

q: A cook follows every coffee step except the last one, 'press ON'. Which part of the definition of a process fails?
options: The steps no longer change anything
The steps together do not reach the goal
The steps are no longer a sequence
The procedure becomes an algorithm
explanation: A process is a sequence of steps that together reach a goal. Without pressing ON, the coffee is never brewed.
